MKT-01-A.conclusion: Partly supported. Singapore teachers spend 6.4 h/week marking (OECD TALIS 2024, MKT-E020) and differentiated primary teaching doubles preparation time (MKT-E017); initial diagnostic assessment adds to primary teachers' workload (MKT-E024), and studies elsewhere show diagnosing maths misconceptions is demanding (MKT-E022, MKT-E023). No evidence specific to tutors or tuition centres.
MKT-01-A.action_reason: Set by Hansle 2026-11-04: teacher time on assessment is supported (TALIS 2024, diagnosis studies); limits stated.

MKT-01-B.conclusion: Partly supported. Automated grading cut teacher grading time by 35% (MKT-E028) and teachers value adaptive diagnostic assessment (MKT-E025); Singapore households spent S$1.8b on tuition in 2023 (MKT-E002). No public evidence that tuition centres pay for diagnostic software; diligence should ask centres about current tool spend.

MKT-01-C.conclusion: Weakly supported. Teachers use dashboards to find struggling students (MKT-E029, MKT-E031) and are open to AI tools (MKT-E030), but all evidence is from schools or universities, none from Singapore tuition centres. Needs primary research (interviews or a pilot) with centres.

MKT-01-D.conclusion: Not established. MOE publishes student counts but no count of tuition centres, and does not track the industry's size. The number of potential centre customers must remain an explicit assumption (F-A01) and an open diligence question.

MKT-02-A.conclusion: Largely contradicted. Geniebook pairs AI gap-tracking with human tutors (MKT-E019, MKT-E008); KooBits sells teacher strength-and-weakness reports to schools (MKT-E041) and offers its system to existing learning centres (MKT-E040); MOE ALS gives teachers a progress and concept-mastery dashboard (MKT-E042) and requires teachers to vet its automated feedback (MKT-E043). Not found in any public material: teacher-reviewed AI gap diagnosis available to tuition centres (ALS is limited to the national school system), or reports that trace each gap to the student's responses.
MKT-02-A.action_reason: Set by Hansle 2026-11-06: reviewed counter-evidence shows competitors already diagnose and report learning gaps, serve learning centres (KooBits) and have teachers vet AI feedback (MOE ALS). Correct the claim to what remains: teacher-reviewed AI gap diagnosis available to tuition centres, and reports that trace each gap to student responses (open diligence question).

MKT-02-B.conclusion: Synthetic by design: MathBridge's features are fictional (SYN-02). Against the Competitor Matrix, the only distinguishing features left are teacher-reviewed AI diagnosis offered to tuition centres and response-level evidence links; a centre licence alone is not unique (KooBits, MKT-E040), nor is teacher review alone (MOE ALS, MKT-E043).

MKT-02-C.conclusion: Indirectly supported. Expert human feedback is more nuanced than AI alone (MKT-E036), human-AI co-produced feedback keeps trust when the source is disclosed while AI-only feedback loses it (MKT-E037), and explained diagnostic results help teachers plan (MKT-E039). No evidence that tuition centres value or would pay for these features.

MKT-01.conclusion: Partly supported. Diagnosis is time-consuming and teachers value time-saving tools (MKT-01-A, -B, -C: PARTIAL), but evidence comes from schools and universities, not Singapore tuition centres, and the number of centres is unknown (MKT-01-D: MISSING, open diligence question). Public evidence describes the market, not MathBridge's traction (fictional, pre-revenue, SYN-05).

MKT-02.conclusion: Not supported as stated. Competitors already diagnose learning gaps, Geniebook combines AI with human tutors, KooBits already serves learning centres, and MOE ALS already has teachers vet AI feedback (MKT-02-A contradicted). MathBridge's remaining difference (teacher-reviewed AI diagnosis for tuition centres, response-level evidence links) is fictional (MKT-02-B) and its value to centres is only indirectly supported (MKT-02-C). Diligence must confirm the difference exists and that centres value it.
